question.text: An electric dipole of dipole moment is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>6</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><mo> </mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> placed in a uniform electric field of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><mo> </mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> in such a way that dipole moment is along electric field. The work done in rotating dipole by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo> </mo></math>in this field will be_______<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>mJ</mi></math>.

solution.text:
The work done for rotating a dipole is given by the change in the potential energy. The potential energy is given by

U=-p→·E→

W =∆U = Uf−Ui

So, the work done is 

 W=-pEcos180°-(-pEcos0°)=2pE=2×6×10-6×1.5×103=18 mJ
